meta.title: Portolan makes geospatial data easy to share and use
meta.description: Portolan is an open specification for publishing geospatial data as plain files in your own storage. No servers, no databases. Browse the catalog registry.

hero.title: Portolan makes geospatial data
hero.description: Portolan is an open-source <spec>specification</spec> and <eco>toolkit</eco> that combines cloud-native file formats with clear metadata and documentation so that people and agents can publish and use data at any scale.

getInvolved.title: Get involved
getInvolved.priority: The simplest way to get started right now is to <publish>publish your data as a Portolan catalog</publish> and let us know how it goes. Feedback on what works, what doesn't, and how Portolan can be improved is always helpful, especially when your implementation differs from existing catalogs.
getInvolved.contributions: We also welcome contributions to the <github>Portolan spec and tooling</github> in the form of bug reports, feature requests, and PRs (and especially PRs). Check out our <issues>open issues</issues> to get started.
getInvolved.community: Portolan is an open-source community project. We welcome new users and contributors. Join the <slack><m>#portolan</m> channel on Slack</slack> and follow the <group>Portolan Google Group</group> for details on our weekly meetings.

open.title: Open and interoperable
open.description: Portolan builds on open standards like <geoparquet><m>GeoParquet</m></geoparquet>, <pmtiles><m>PMTiles</m></pmtiles>, <cog><m>COG</m></cog>, and <stac><m>STAC</m></stac> so that data can be dropped right into tools like QGIS, ArcGIS, Pandas, or BigQuery.

simple.title: Simple, cheap, scalable, sovereign
simple.description: With Portolan, your data are just files in a cloud bucket. Store them with any <m>S3</m>-compatible provider, in any jurisdiction you choose. Your only costs are storage and egress. Scale from megabytes to petabytes with no servers, databases, or custom APIs.

agents.title: Built for people and agents
agents.description: Portolan catalogs are well-structured, well-formatted, and well-documented, so people and agents can find, understand, and use them. Browse the registry yourself to discover new data, or point an agent at the registry and see what it can do.

large.title: Large publishers
large.today: Large archives, such as satellite imagery or national-scale geoportals, are expensive to store and hard to maintain.
large.change: Portolan makes it straightforward to publish that data <cost>as cheaply as possible</cost>, without servers, databases, or APIs, while making it easier to discover and use.

small.title: Small publishers
small.today: Many city governments, NGOs, and other smaller data producers can't afford the cost or complexity of publishing data with tools like GeoServer or Esri.
small.change: Portolan lowers the barrier to entry by letting you share your data with nothing more than a cloud storage bucket.

users.title: Data users
users.today: Most geospatial data is scattered, poorly documented, and stored in ways that make it hard to use.
users.change: Portolan requires clear metadata and documentation, uses formats designed for direct access, and provides a <reg>central registry</reg> of public catalogs. You spend less time finding, downloading, and wrangling data, and more time putting it to work.

howItWorks.title: How it works
howItWorks.intro: Use the <cli>Portolan CLI</cli> or <skills>agent skills</skills> to transform your existing data into a Portolan catalog.

convert.title: Convert
convert.description: Whether you're working with Shapefiles and GeoPackages, a WFS endpoint, or an Esri server, your data end up as <m>GeoParquet</m> and <m>PMTiles</m> for vector and <m>COG</m> for raster.

catalog.title: Catalog
catalog.description: Your cloud-optimized data are organized as a <m>STAC</m> catalog with clear metadata and docs, making the catalog easy to find, understand, and use for people and agents.

publish.title: Publish
publish.description: Your catalog is published to any S3-compatible storage, such as AWS, GCS, Hetzner, or MinIO, with no servers or APIs to set up.

use.title: Use
use.description: Your data can now be dropped directly into tools like QGIS, ArcGIS, or Python, or you can pass the catalog URL to an agent and let it get to work.

demo.title: A better way to work with geospatial data
demo.blurb: Start with real questions, not a script. Watch an agent find relevant catalogs in the Portolan registry and answer complex, natural-language questions about flood risk in Moldova.
demo.captionPhiladelphia: Making <catalog>a Portolan catalog</catalog> start to finish from Philadelphia housing data.
demo.transcriptPhiladelphia: A terminal-only recording shows an agent create and publish a Portolan catalog from ten Open Data Philly datasets. The request names property parcels, land use, zoning base districts and overlays, zoning descriptions, vacant-property indicators, City Council districts, building footprints, and affordable housing production. The agent loads the Portolan bootstrap skill, researches and downloads the sources, enriches metadata, creates thumbnails and map styles, validates the catalog, and publishes it. The terminal reports about 1.78 million features and that all catalog gates pass. It also records unresolved source fields, license details, and upstream tool issues before it syncs the published catalog files and agent guides.
demo.transcriptFloodRisk: A terminal-only recording shows an agent find data about flood risk in Chisinau through the live Portolan registry. It inspects the Moldova geodata catalog and related catalogs for flood extents, flood depth, buildings, population, land cover, hydrography, roads, utilities, and boundaries. It reports Moldova flood scenarios for 1%, 0.5%, and 0.1% annual probabilities, dam-breach extents, JRC GLOFAS depth layers, and GHSL population grids. It then calculates screening estimates for exposed buildings and population, and ranks several planning corridors. The result notes that the estimates lack local depth, velocity, arrival time, and building-vulnerability data.

ecosystem.title: Ecosystem
ecosystem.intro: The Portolan specification can be implemented in a number of ways. Here is a list of core, community-contributed, and commercial tools to make publishing and working with Portolan data easy.
ecosystem.empty: No tools in this tier yet.

commercial.title: Commercial products on the open core
commercial.body: Portolan standardizes the published catalog, not the software around it, so companies can sell capabilities the open tools do not cover. <carto>CARTO SDI</carto> extends Portolan for organizations with private datasets, governance and audits, dataset commercialization, and writable datasets. If a product goes away, the catalog keeps working and another tool can take over.

registry.title: Portolan registry
registry.intro: The <reg>Portolan registry</reg> is a catalog of independently hosted catalogs and a first step toward a federated network for geospatial data. It makes interoperable catalogs from many publishers searchable in one place while the underlying data remain distributed and are queried directly from the source.
registry.note: Some of these catalogs are unofficial mirrors maintained by volunteers. We expect mirrors to be replaced by official catalogs as publishers adopt the Portolan specification.

meta.title: Frequently asked questions
meta.description: Answers to common questions about Portolan. How it relates to STAC and cloud-optimized formats, why it does not need a serving layer, what conformance guarantees, and what it cannot do yet.

standards.q: Isn’t Portolan just STAC and cloud-optimized formats?
standards.p1: Portolan builds directly on STAC, GeoParquet, COG, PMTiles, and related standards. The difference is that those standards intentionally leave many implementation choices open, while Portolan defines and validates a quality floor for publishing geospatial data well.
standards.p2: For example, Portolan requires GeoParquet to be spatially ordered and include spatial statistics that let clients skip irrelevant row groups. It requires COGs to include useful overviews and embedded statistics, and requires hosted assets to support HTTP range requests and browser access through CORS. The goal is not just to use cloud-native formats in name, but to use them in ways that reliably deliver the performance and ergonomics they are supposed to provide.
standards.p3: See the <spec>Portolan specification</spec> and <rashid>rashid</rashid>, the Portolan validator.

servers.q: Why not just use GeoServer, PostGIS, or an OGC API?
servers.p1: For public, read-heavy data, Portolan is based on the idea that a dedicated serving layer is usually unnecessary.
servers.p2: Modern clients can work directly with cloud-optimized files. DuckDB can query remote Parquet and GeoParquet with filtering, joins, and spatial operations. QGIS, BigQuery, Sedona, and other tools can work with the same underlying data. Portolan can also publish PMTiles and styles so interactive web maps do not need an on-demand tile server. You can still put an API, database, or application service on top when a particular use case needs one. Portolan removes the requirement that every dataset depend on one just to be accessible.

capabilities.q: What can cloud-native files do that used to require an API?
capabilities.p2: Cloud-optimized formats are designed for efficient partial access over the network. Instead of downloading an entire dataset or sending every request through a server-side subsetting service, clients can fetch only the portions of a file they need and work with them directly.
capabilities.p3: That means many capabilities traditionally associated with APIs can happen on top of the files themselves. Tools such as DuckDB, BigQuery, and Sedona can filter, join, subset, and analyze Parquet and GeoParquet directly. COG readers can request only the raster tiles and resolutions needed for a particular view, while PMTiles can serve interactive maps without an on-demand tile server.
capabilities.p4: Portolan is designed around this model: publish data in formats that support efficient direct access, and let users choose the tools that query, analyze, or visualize them. A service can still be added when a workflow genuinely needs server-side behavior, but it no longer has to sit between every user and every dataset.
capabilities.p5: Access-controlled data is planned for Portolan v1.0. Transactional editing is not yet supported.

conformance.q: What does Portolan conformance actually guarantee?
conformance.p1: A catalog does not conform simply because it declares the Portolan extension. It conforms only if it passes the Portolan validator, which checks the STAC structure, Portolan metadata requirements, and requirements that can only be verified by inspecting the data itself.
conformance.p2: That includes things such as GeoParquet spatial ordering, row-group statistics, and embedded COG statistics. Conformance therefore means more than valid metadata: it gives users and software a stronger guarantee that the data are structured, hosted, documented, and optimized in predictable ways.

lockIn.q: Does Portolan replace one proprietary platform with another?
lockIn.p1: Avoiding that is a core part of the architecture. Portolan standardizes the published catalog, not the cloud provider, publishing workflow, user interface, analytical engine, or commercial vendor around it.
lockIn.p2: If a commercial product creates and manages a Portolan catalog and you later stop using that product, the published catalog still works and another tool, provider, or vendor can take over. The goal is an ecosystem of competing, interoperable implementations rather than a vertically integrated Portolan platform.

dataModel.q: Does Portolan standardize my data model?
dataModel.p1: No. Portolan standardizes how data are packaged, documented, hosted, and accessed. It does not prescribe one universal schema for roads, buildings, parcels, administrative boundaries, or other domain data.
dataModel.p2: Semantic standards and shared schemas can sit on top of Portolan where they are useful. Portolan addresses a different layer of interoperability: making differently produced datasets consistently discoverable, queryable, documented, and usable with common tools.

agents.q: Why are agents part of a data publishing specification?
agents.p1: Agents are becoming another major class of data user, and that changes some of the assumptions behind public data infrastructure.
agents.p2: Agents can inspect and query many datasets quickly, so Portolan assumes catalogs will be consumed programmatically at scale. Every catalog and collection therefore includes an <m>AGENTS.md</m> file that can document access patterns, useful queries, data-quality notes, schema conventions, and other guidance that helps software use the data correctly.
agents.p3: Agents are not required to publish or consume Portolan data. The CLI provides a deterministic publishing workflow, and standard tools can use the resulting catalogs directly. Agent-readiness is a design requirement, not a dependency on any particular AI system.

gaps.p1: Portolan is still early-stage, and the specification and tooling are evolving as we test them against more publishers, datasets, and use cases. Current gaps include access-controlled data, transactional editing workflows, and normative support for formats such as Zarr and COPC.
gaps.p2: Our near-term focus is to expand the set of reference catalogs, stabilize the core specification, and reach a stable v1.0 CLI. Breaking changes remain possible until then, so Portolan is currently best suited to early adopters. See the <roadmap>project roadmap</roadmap> for current work and linked issues.

name.p1: Portolan charts were among the earliest practical navigational maps. Chartmakers built these working tools from sailors' observations and corrected them as new voyages added evidence.
name.p2: No single authority made them. Workshops in different ports refined them as sailors brought new observations. Their shared visual language let sailors use each chart across ports and nations.
name.p3: The project takes its name from that tradition. A Portolan catalog is a practical tool, not an academic exercise. It holds open-format files in the publisher's storage for people and agents across organizations, clouds, and borders.
